note: Curated flag sets. Availability (`availableIn`) is filled in by tools/build-dataset.mjs from the extracted GCC data, so a flag is never advertised for a release that does not have it.

references.label: OpenSSF — Compiler Options Hardening Guide for C and C++
Red Hat — Recommended compiler and linker flags for GCC

profiles.name: Hardening — Baseline
profiles.summary: The OpenSSF baseline: exploit mitigations every production build on GNU/Linux should carry. Negligible runtime cost.
profiles.description: A conservative, widely deployed set of mitigations. These flags are what most distributions already build their packages with, so they are well tested and rarely break working code. Combine with `-O2` or higher — `_FORTIFY_SOURCE` needs optimisation to see object sizes.

flags.why: Required for `_FORTIFY_SOURCE` to compute object sizes, and enables most `-Wmaybe-*` analyses.
Replaces unbounded libc calls (`memcpy`, `sprintf`, …) with checked variants that abort on overflow.
Places a canary in functions with local arrays or address-taken locals, catching stack smashing at return.
Probes every page when growing the stack so a huge frame cannot jump over the guard page into the heap.
Emits Intel CET landing pads and shadow-stack support, breaking ROP/JOP gadget chains on capable hardware.
Position independent code, the prerequisite for a full-ASLR executable.
Produces a position independent executable so the main image is randomised too.
Marks the GOT and other relocations read-only after startup.
Resolves all symbols at load time so the GOT can actually be sealed by RELRO.
Refuses an executable stack even if one translation unit forgot the `.note.GNU-stack` marker.
Fails the link on unresolved symbols in shared libraries instead of deferring the crash to runtime.
Turns non-literal format strings into a hard error — the classic remote code execution primitive.
An implicitly declared function silently truncates 64-bit return values; make it fatal.

profiles.name: Hardening — Strict
profiles.summary: Everything in the baseline plus the aggressive mitigations. Measurable runtime cost; validate before shipping.
profiles.description: For code that parses untrusted input. Several of these flags require recent GCC releases (`-fstrict-flex-arrays` needs GCC 13, `-ftrivial-auto-var-init` GCC 12, `-fzero-call-used-regs` GCC 11) — use the version filter to see which ones your toolchain has. `_FORTIFY_SOURCE=3` needs GCC 12 and glibc 2.35+.

flags.why: Baseline requirement for the fortified libc wrappers.
Uses `__builtin_dynamic_object_size`, so bounds are checked even for dynamically sized buffers.
Canary in *every* function, not just the ones with arrays.
Stack guard page cannot be skipped.
Forward and backward edge control-flow integrity via CET.
Only `[]` counts as a flexible array member, so `[0]` and `[1]` trailing arrays get real bounds checks.
Zero-initialises automatic variables, removing uninitialised-memory information leaks.
Scrubs registers on return, shrinking the pool of usable ROP gadgets.
Keeps defensive `if (!p)` tests the optimiser would otherwise delete after a prior dereference.
Signed overflow wraps instead of being undefined, so overflow checks written in C keep working.
Disables type-based alias analysis, which frequently miscompiles hand-rolled serialisation code.
Keeps unwind tables so stack traces and cancellation still work in hardened C code.
Prerequisite for a PIE executable.
Full ASLR for the main image.
Read-only relocations.
Eager binding, required for full RELRO.
Non-executable stack.
Prevents the object from being loaded with `dlopen`, a common injection vector.
Drops unused DT_NEEDED entries, shrinking the attack surface of the dependency graph.

profiles.name: Diagnostics — Recommended
profiles.summary: The warnings that actually find bugs, without drowning an existing codebase in noise.
profiles.description: A pragmatic superset of `-Wall -Wextra`. Everything here has a low false-positive rate on real code; the remaining noise usually points at something worth fixing anyway.

flags.why: The core set — see the *Umbrella* filter for exactly which options it turns on in your release.
The second tier: unused parameters, sign compares, misleading indentation.
Flags GNU extensions, keeping the code portable to other compilers.
Adds `-Wformat-nonliteral`, `-Wformat-security` and `-Wformat-y2k` on top of `-Wformat`.
Shadowed variables are a classic source of "I edited the wrong one" bugs.
Catches casts that silently drop `const` or `volatile`.
Pointer casts that increase alignment requirements trap on strict-alignment targets.
Implicit narrowing conversions — the root of many integer-overflow CVEs.
Signed/unsigned conversions that change the value.
Accidental `float` → `double` promotion, a real cost on embedded FPUs.
`#if FOO` where `FOO` is undefined silently evaluates to 0.
Gives string literals `const char[]` type so writes are diagnosed.
Arithmetic on `void *` / function pointers is a GNU extension with surprising sizes.
Variable length arrays put attacker-controlled sizes on the stack.
Missing `break` in a `switch` — the bug behind more than one CVE.
Repeated conditions in an `if`/`else if` chain, almost always a copy-paste error.
Identical bodies on both branches of an `if`.
Suspicious uses of logical operators where bitwise was meant.
Paths where a null pointer is dereferenced.
C only: `f()` is not a prototype and disables argument checking.
C only: K&R definitions bypass parameter type checking.
C only: a public function with no visible prototype cannot be type-checked at call sites.
Duplicate declarations usually mean a header was reorganised badly.

profiles.name: Diagnostics — Zero Tolerance
profiles.summary: Warnings as errors, plus the static analyzer. For new code and CI gates.
profiles.description: Only realistic on a codebase that starts clean, or behind a dedicated CI job. `-fanalyzer` (GCC 10+) does interprocedural symbolic execution and is slow — run it separately from the normal build.

flags.why: Baseline.
Second tier.
Strict ISO conformance.
Every warning becomes a build failure.
No silent narrowing.
No silent sign changes.
Full format string checking.
Every enumerator must be handled explicitly.
Exact floating point comparison is almost always wrong.
Reports every optimisation that assumes signed overflow cannot happen.
Tells you which functions the stack protector could *not* cover.
Nested functions requiring executable stack trampolines.
No shadowing at all.
GCC 10+: path-sensitive analysis for double-free, use-after-free, leaks and taint.

profiles.name: Sanitizers — Address & UB
profiles.summary: Instrumented build for test suites and fuzzing. Never ship this to production.
profiles.description: ASan and UBSan catch at runtime what no amount of static analysis will. Expect roughly 2× slowdown and 3× memory. `-fno-sanitize-recover=all` makes the first violation abort, which is what you want in CI. ASan and TSan cannot be combined.

flags.why: Enough optimisation to keep tests fast without destroying stack traces.
Full debug info, including macros, so reports point at real source.
Out-of-bounds, use-after-free, use-after-return, leaks.
Signed overflow, bad shifts, misaligned access, invalid casts.
Bounds checking that also covers trailing arrays.
Abort on the first violation instead of logging and continuing.
Keeps stack traces readable.
Tentative definitions become real symbols so ASan can guard them.

profiles.name: Sanitizers — Threads
profiles.summary: Data race detection. Mutually exclusive with AddressSanitizer.
profiles.description: ThreadSanitizer instruments every memory access and models the happens-before graph. Roughly 5–15× slowdown, so point it at a targeted concurrency test suite rather than the whole build.

flags.why: Keeps the instrumented binary usable.
Race reports need line numbers on both accesses.
Detects data races and some misuse of the pthread API.
Readable stacks for both sides of a race.
TSan requires position independent code.
TSan requires a PIE executable.

profiles.name: Embedded — Freestanding
profiles.summary: Bare-metal and firmware: no hosted libc assumptions, deterministic size, hardening that costs no runtime.
profiles.description: For firmware there is no dynamic loader, so ASLR and RELRO are meaningless; what matters is stack discipline, deterministic layout and not letting the optimiser assume a hosted environment.

flags.why: Optimise for size — usually the binding constraint on flash.
No hosted libc: `main` is not special and builtins are not assumed.
Catches duplicate globals at link time instead of silently merging them.
Stops GCC from turning your loop into a `memcpy` that does not exist on the target.
Cheap stack smashing detection; needs a `__stack_chk_fail` implementation.
Emits per-function stack usage so worst-case stack depth can be computed.
Fails loudly when a function eats more stack than the budget allows.
Same idea, per frame.
One section per object so the linker can drop unused data.
One section per function, prerequisite for `--gc-sections`.
Garbage collects unreferenced sections — often 20–40% smaller images.
No startup files or standard libraries; the firmware provides its own.

profiles.name: Reproducible Builds
profiles.summary: Byte-identical output regardless of build directory, hostname or timestamp.
profiles.description: The remaining sources of nondeterminism after these flags are `__DATE__`/`__TIME__` in the source itself and the ordering of inputs on the command line. See reproducible-builds.org for the full checklist.

flags.why: Rewrites the build directory out of debug info, `__FILE__` and coverage data in one flag (GCC 8+).
The debug-info-only subset, for toolchains without `-ffile-prefix-map`.
Makes internally generated symbol names deterministic instead of derived from the file name and time.
Warns on `__DATE__`, `__TIME__` and `__TIMESTAMP__`, the usual culprits.
Removes a heuristic that has historically depended on hash table ordering.
Drops the build ID, which otherwise hashes inputs including paths.

profiles.name: Release — Performance
profiles.summary: A fast, still-debuggable release build. No fast-math, no UB gambling.
profiles.description: `-O3` is not automatically faster than `-O2` — measure. LTO usually pays for itself. Deliberately excludes `-ffast-math`, which changes floating point results and breaks NaN handling.

flags.why: The best tested optimisation level; `-O3` only after benchmarking.
Cross translation unit inlining and dead code removal.
Lets shared libraries inline their own calls; large win for C++ libraries.
Smaller dynamic symbol table, faster loading, better LTO.
Calls through the GOT directly, avoiding the PLT indirection.
Debug info costs nothing at runtime and makes production crashes actionable.
Required for cheap stack sampling by `perf` in production.
Asks the linker to optimise the hash table layout.
Fewer runtime dependencies, faster startup.

profiles.name: Debug — Developer Build
profiles.summary: Optimised for stepping through code and getting truthful stack traces.
profiles.description: `-Og` is the level designed for debugging: it applies optimisations that do not interfere with the debugger. `-O0` is only worth it when even `-Og` reorders something you need to watch.

flags.why: Debug-friendly optimisation: fast enough to run, faithful enough to step through.
Level 3 keeps macro definitions so `print SOME_MACRO` works in GDB.
Unbroken backtraces.
Every frame you expect actually appears in the trace.
Keeps variable locations accurate through optimisation.
Turns on libstdc++ precondition checks: bounds on `operator[]`, valid iterators.
The full libstdc++ debug mode. Changes the ABI, so rebuild everything.
